opus-5.5.text:
For me, pretraining is where the model's core capabilities actually come from. Post-training matters a lot. It shapes behavior, it makes the model follow instructions, it unlocks reasoning in a way users can feel. But in many ways it's drawing out what's already latent in the base model. If the knowledge, the world model, the raw ability to generalize isn't there after pretraining, post-training can't really create it from scratch.

So what pulls me in is that pretraining feels closer to the fundamental question: how does intelligence emerge from data and compute at all? You're dealing with scaling laws, data mixtures, architecture choices, optimization stability at enormous scale. Every decision compounds over trillions of tokens, and small insights can shift the whole capability frontier. It's very empirical but also very principled. You can form hypotheses, test them at small scale, and see whether they extrapolate.

There's also a certain humility to it that I like. In post-training you often get fast feedback and you can see a behavior change almost immediately. In pretraining the feedback loop is slower and the signal is noisier, so you have to think carefully about what you're measuring and why. That forces you to build better intuitions and better science.

And honestly, I think there's still a lot of headroom. People sometimes say pretraining is "done" or that the data wall is coming, but I see it differently. How we use data, how we construct it, how efficiently models learn from it: those are still wide open problems. That sense of unexplored territory is a big part of what keeps me excited.

r001.rationale: The response presents pretraining as building the model’s core capabilities and post-training as shaping behavior and drawing out what is latent in the base model.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's because pretraining is where the model actually gets its knowledge. Everything the model knows about the world, about code, about language, about how things relate to each other, comes from that phase. Post-training is important, but it's mostly shaping and surfacing what's already there. You're teaching the model how to behave, how to follow instructions, how to be helpful. You're not really teaching it much that's new.

And I find the pretraining problem more fundamental, in a way. It's a question of what you feed the model, how you order it, how you scale the data and the compute together, and what architecture decisions let you get the most out of a fixed budget. Those decisions compound. If you get the data mix wrong, or the tokenizer is bad, or you under-train on some domain, no amount of post-training will fix that. It becomes a ceiling.

There's also something about the feedback loop that I like. In post-training you get signal quickly, you can run an experiment, look at evals, iterate in a day. Pretraining is slower and more expensive, and the cost of a mistake is much higher. So you have to be more careful, more principled, and more willing to build small-scale experiments that actually predict what happens at scale. That discipline suits me. I like problems where you have to think hard before you spend the money.

And finally, I'd say the frontier still moves most when pretraining moves. The big jumps we've seen in capability, the things that made people's jaws drop, mostly came from bigger or better pretrained base models. Post-training made them usable, but the raw capability was born earlier. I want to be close to where that capability comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining is where the model gets its knowledge and describes post-training as shaping and surfacing what is already there, clearly making the requested distinction.

astra-6.text:
What draws me to pretraining is that you’re working on the foundation of the model’s capabilities. You have this relatively simple objective, but the choices around data, architecture, and optimization can lead to surprisingly different behavior. I find that relationship really interesting: what does the model learn, and why does it learn that from this particular setup?

Post-training is fascinating too, because it shapes how those capabilities become useful. But I’m especially drawn to the question of where the capabilities come from in the first place. Pretraining gives you a way to investigate that directly.

r001.rationale: The response presents pretraining as building the foundation and producing capabilities, while post-training shapes how those capabilities become useful.

sol-6.1.text:
What draws me to pretraining is that you’re working on the foundation of the model’s capabilities. You’re asking what it can learn from data, how effectively it can learn it, and what changes when you scale. I find that combination of scientific questions and engineering challenges really compelling.

Post-training is fascinating too, because it shapes how those capabilities become useful. But with pretraining, the feedback feels more fundamental: if an experiment works, you’ve changed what the model is able to build on. That’s the part I’m especially drawn to.

r001.rationale: It presents pretraining as changing the model’s foundation and capabilities, while post-training shapes how those capabilities become useful—an equivalent distinction between improving the underlying material and shaping it.
